extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners reading MPEP guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing and documenting 35 U.S.C. §101 subject-matter eligibility analyses and rejections (Alice/Mayo framework) for patent claims, including when to use streamlined analysis and how to explain and support rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-of-use / technological-environment limitations generally insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that merely specify a technological environment or field of use (e.g., execution on a generic computer, use within a telephone network or the Internet, data related to a particular domain like the power grid, or implementing budgeting/advertising on the Internet) do not meaningfully limit an abstract idea and therefore typically do not render the claim patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an explanation in a rejection why such limitations do not meaningfully limit the claim. Examples: Flook (industry-limited math), FairWarning v. Iatric (computer execution), Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec (telephone/Internet), Electric Power Group (power-grid data), Genetic Techs. Ltd. v. Merial (informing doctors to apply law of nature), Ultramercial (advertising on Internet), buySAFE v. Google (computer/network use). Note: courts often use “technological environment” and “field of use” interchangeably. Consider overlap with insignificant extra-solution activity (MPEP §2106.05(g)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined eligibility analysis (Pathway A) for self-evident eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may use a streamlined eligibility analysis when the eligibility of the claim is self-evident (e.g., the claim clearly improves technology or computer functionality), but the result must be the same as the full Alice/Mayo analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only use when eligibility is clear; if there is doubt whether the claim seeks coverage of a judicial exception, perform the full analysis. The streamlined analysis is not a way to avoid findings of ineligibility. The record may simply reflect eligibility by absence of a 101 rejection or by clarifying remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility is self-evident (Pathway A) — criteria and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that, when viewed as a whole, clearly do not tie up any judicial exception or clearly improve technology/computer functionality may be eligible without a full analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include a complex manufactured industrial product or process with meaningful limitations, a robotic arm assembly with control system using mathematical relationships (not attempting to tie up the math), or a product that includes incidental nature-based components (e.g., cellphone with gold contact). Such claims do not require a markedly different characteristics analysis for product-of-nature issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear improvement to technology/computer functionality avoids full analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are directed to clear improvements to computer-related technology or functionality (i.e., not abstract when appropriately claimed) may avoid full Alice/Mayo analysis and be found eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Enfish (self-referential table), McRO (automatic lip synchronization/animation) as examples. If a claim is a 'close call' (e.g., BASCOM filtering content), perform the full analysis. It may be reasonable for an examiner to find such claims eligible at Pathway A or at Step 2A/2B depending on facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base eligibility rejections on substantive law and precedent; explain prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility rejections must be grounded in 35 U.S.C. §101 as interpreted by judicial precedent and must set forth a prima facie case of ineligibility so the applicant has sufficient notice and can effectively respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review the substantive law in MPEP §§2106.03–2106.06. The examiner's initial burden is to clearly and specifically explain why a claim is ineligible. Even if relying on training or examples, those do not themselves constitute the legal basis for a rejection—cite substantive precedent and reasoned rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate eligibility on a claim-by-claim basis and review the entire record
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine eligibility for each claim separately by reviewing the specification, claims, prosecution history, and relevant case law or prior art before concluding whether the claimed invention is patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependent claims may be eligible even if an independent claim is ineligible (they may add limitations that integrate the exception). Conversely, dependent claims can be ineligible if they add judicial exceptions without integrating them. Consider each claim on its own merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and explain the judicial exception recited in the claim (Step 2A Prong One)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection must point to the specific claim limitation(s) that recite or describe the judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon, product of nature) and explain why those limitations are considered an exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For abstract ideas, identify the abstract idea as recited and explain why it falls within one of the enumerated groupings (mathematical concepts, mental processes, certain methods of organizing human activity) per MPEP §2106.04(a)(2), or justify a 'tentative abstract idea' under MPEP §2106.04(a)(3). Avoid relying on non-precedential decisions unless facts match. Provide a reasoned rationale; sample explanations are provided (e.g., comparing to a threshold is a mental process).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify additional claim elements and explain why they do not integrate the exception or add significantly more (Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: After identifying the judicial exception, the rejection must identify claim features/limitations beyond the exception and explain why these additional elements, individually and in combination, do not integrate the exception into a practical application or amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address elements both individually and as a combination. Remember that a new combination of known steps may be patent eligible (Diamond v. Diehr). Explain the rationale supporting the conclusion so the applicant can respond. See MPEP §2106.05 for detailed considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support assertions that elements are well-understood, routine, conventional (Step 2B) with specified evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: If asserting that particular claim limitations are well-understood, routine, or conventional in the relevant field (a Step 2B factual finding), the examiner must expressly support the rejection in writing with one or more of the prescribed evidentiary bases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitted supports: (A) citation to an express statement in the specification or a prosecution statement showing the element is well-understood/routine/conventional; (B) citation to one or more court decisions that note the conventional nature of the element(s) (ensure claim language and level of generality match); (C) citation to a publication (book, manual, review article) demonstrating the element is well-known and in common use. A specification's silence alone is insufficient to establish conventionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary standards differ by analysis step
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2A Prong One (identifying an exception) requires a reasoned rationale and does not require evidence; Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B may require evidence when asserting that additional elements are well-understood, routine, or conventional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts treat eligibility as a legal question that may have underlying factual issues (e.g., Berkheimer). For Step 2A Prong One, a reasoned rationale suffices (no affidavit/publication required). For Step 2B, do not assert conventionality without providing the required support (options A–C).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer components/functions at high level often insufficient to add 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim limitations that recite generic computer components performing generic computer functions at a high level (e.g., using the Internet to gather data) typically do not meaningfully limit an abstract idea and thus do not add significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why these generic computing functions do not meaningfully limit the claim. However, courts have found combinations of generic components to perform non-generic functions and thereby be significantly more (DDR Holdings). See MPEP §§2106.05(f) and 2106.05(d) for more on generic computing functions and well-understood/routine elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address insignificant extra-solution activity and Flook/Parker restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering) or limitations that only generally link the judicial exception to a technological environment are often 'insignificant' and do not meaningfully limit the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why the extra-solution activity or field-of-use limitation does not integrate the exception or add significantly more. Examples: adding storing data to a process of computing a mathematical area; limiting a mathematical formula to particular industries (Flook). See MPEP §§2106.05(g) and 2106.05(h).

rubrics_metrics.name: When issuing a rejection, suggest claim amendments from the specification when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: If a rejection is made, it is best practice for the examiner to consult the specification to determine if there are elements that could be added to the claim to make it eligible and identify those elements in the Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify specific specification elements and suggest them as ways to overcome the rejection, thereby clarifying possible paths for applicant amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact prosecution: perform and state complete examination under other patentability statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Regardless of a 35 U.S.C. §101 rejection, examiners should perform a complete examination of every claim under other patentability requirements (35 U.S.C. §§102, 103, 112, utility, inventorship, double patenting, and non-statutory double patenting) and state all non-cumulative reasons for rejecting claims in the first Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State all non-cumulative rejections and bases in the first Office action to support compact prosecution and provide the applicant with a complete picture of patentability issues.
